comments.author: @angelaberni8873
comments.text: It's such a shame that many foreigners consider Italian cuisine to be only pasta and pizza. They have NO IDEA of the variations of food from not only one region to another,but also from one village to the next. When in Italy I BEG you to find out what are the local regional dishes . Ask shop owners where is a family run " trattoria". They are usually a few streets behind the main tourists walks. DON'T for goodness sake eat where there are huge menus posted outside. I repeat....every region has their own specialities. Try those and I guarantee that ,those meals will remain in your memories forever. They may very well convince you to move to Italy 😂. So what are you waiting for....sell up and join us in the most beautiful, welcoming country in the world. If I can't convince you,this video certainly can. Ciao ❤

replies.author: @HappyTravel99
replies.text: What a wonderful invitation to experience the real Italy! We especially love your advice about exploring small, family-run trattorias away from the tourist streets. Sometimes the most unforgettable memories come from a simple meal in a little village. Italy is so much more than its famous landmarks, and your passion for your country really shines through! Hopefully, your comment and our video will inspire more people to discover that side of Italy. Ciao, and thank you for sharing such a lovely perspective! ❤️

comments.author: @ExploreTravelDocs
comments.text: I’ve traveled a lot, but I’ve always held off on visiting Italy, assuming it would just feel like one big, crowded tourist attraction. This video is making me seriously rethink that! For the locals and past visitors: is it actually easy to find this slow, authentic village life, or do you really have to go out of your way to escape the tourist traps? Would love to hear your honest take!

replies.author: @ExploreTravelDocs
replies.text:
@enricacantori2984 That’s a fair point, and I probably chose the wrong words there. 😊 I didn’t mean to reduce Italy to a “tourist attraction”—quite the opposite. What draws me to Italy is exactly what you described: the history, culture, art, and especially the everyday life that exists beyond the places millions of visitors come to see. 🇮🇹

As a local, your perspective is exactly what I was hoping to hear. I’d much rather discover the Italy people actually live in than only the Italy tourists usually see. ❤

replies.author: @enricacantori2984
replies.text: "Attrazione turistica"? Tutto quello che attira milioni di turisti è patrimonio della cultura, della storia, dell' arte mondiale: ci sono tanti modi di vedere queste meraviglie quando non ci sono i turisti (che poi saresti tu!) Se sei pigro e non ti informi come muoverti, sì, è meglio se non vieni.

comments.author: @Sailingveterinarian
comments.text: A beautiful, well made video. Great explanations of the simple things that make Italia special. I was fortunate to go to veterinary school in Parma for 5 years. Lived in compania on a horse farm and experienced the real life, without tourism. Heading next month to Sardinia and Calabria. Speaking Italian makes it very special exploring the small villages.

replies.author: @Sailingveterinarian
replies.text: Of course we also experienced the other real part of Italia…the bureaucracy…registering for the university, the classes, paying of fees, buying and registering a car….francoboli for everything…

replies.author: @Sailingveterinarian
replies.text: ⁠We had a house to stay in, in exchange for caring for the horses. We worked in the fields with our neighbors, baling hay, milking cows, and wine making. Great camaraderie. Great experiences, and also a wonderful education.  Definitely feels more like home to me than anywhere else.

replies.author: @HappyTravel99
replies.text: What a wonderful experience — five years in Parma and living on a horse farm in Campania must have given you a very special view of everyday Italian life beyond the usual tourist routes. Sardinia and Calabria should be another amazing chapter, especially when you can speak Italian and connect with people in the smaller villages. Thank you so much for sharing your story, and I hope you have a beautiful journey next month. Please keep watching, and don’t forget to like and subscribe if you enjoy our documentaries!
